parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: wavelength of maximum intensity is inversely proportional to (thermodynamic) temperature

hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens to the peak of a black-body curve when a star gets hotter - does the brightest wavelength shift to shorter or longer wavelengths, and how is it linked to temperature in kelvin?
parts.proper_answer: The wavelength $\lambda_{max}$ of maximum intensity is inversely proportional to the thermodynamic temperature $T$, so $\lambda_{max}T = \text{constant}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Peak Colour to Temperature**
Imagine heating a piece of metal. It first glows red, then orange, then white-blue. Hotter means more energy per photon, so the peak of emission moves to shorter wavelength. For stars, which are close to black bodies, the same idea applies.

Step 2: **State the Law Precisely**
You can say this in words as an inverse proportion: $$ \lambda_{max} \propto \frac{1}{T} $$ where $\lambda_{max}$ is the wavelength of maximum emission rate and $T$ must be the thermodynamic (Kelvin) temperature. Equivalently $$ \lambda_{max}T = \text{constant} $$

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
Fig. 10.1 shows the wavelength distributions of electromagnetic radiation emitted by two stars A and B.

{{figure:figure_10_1}}

Fig. 10.1

The surface temperature of star A is known to be $5800\text{ K}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Determine the surface temperature of star B.

markscheme_points.text: λMAX = 0.50 μm for A and 0.65 μm for B

hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the tops of the two curves in Fig. 10.1 and read off the wavelength where the rate of emission is greatest for star A and for star B.
Hint 2: Since $\lambda_{max}T$ is the same for both stars, set up a ratio using the known $5800\text{ K}$ for star A to find the unknown $T$ for star B.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the Peaks from the Graph**
The peak is where each curve is highest. For star A the top is at about $$ \lambda_{max,A} \approx 0.50\,\mu\text{m} $$ For the dashed star B curve the top is shifted to the right at about $$ \lambda_{max,B} \approx 0.65\,\mu\text{m} $$ Longer peak wavelength already tells you B is cooler.

Step 2: **Use the Constant Product**
Wien's law gives the same constant for both: $$ \lambda_{max,A}T_A = \lambda_{max,B}T_B $$ Rearrange before putting numbers in: $$ T_B = T_A \times \frac{\lambda_{max,A}}{\lambda_{max,B}} $$ Then: $$ T_B = 5800 \times \frac{0.50}{0.65} \approx 4460\text{ K} \approx 4500\text{ K} $$ Keep 2 significant figures to match the graph reading.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
Star B appears less bright than star A when viewed from the Earth.

Use Fig. 10.1 to suggest, with a reason, how else the physical appearance of star B compares with that of star A.

markscheme_points.text: (star B has) greater peak / average wavelength

hints: Hint 1: Apart from height (brightness), compare the horizontal positions of the two peaks in Fig. 10.1 - which star emits most strongly at longer wavelengths?
Hint 2: Recall how wavelength relates to perceived colour across the visible spectrum, from blue at short wavelength to red at long wavelength.
parts.proper_answer: Star B has a greater peak (average) wavelength than star A, so star B appears redder than star A.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Compare Average Wavelength**
Brightness is the height or area of the curve, but colour depends on where the curve is centred left to right. Fig. 10.1 shows the peak for B at ~$0.65\,\mu\text{m}$ compared with ~$0.50\,\mu\text{m}$ for A. So B emits a larger fraction of its light at longer wavelengths.

Step 2: **Translate to Colour**
Longer visible wavelength means redder light, shorter means bluer. Because B is cooler, its distribution is shifted toward the red end. So as well as looking dimmer, star B looks redder (or more orange) than star A.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem: The lines in Fig. 10.1 have been corrected for redshift.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text: State what is meant by redshift.

markscheme_points.text: apparent wavelength is greater or wavelength is greater than known value
(due to) movement of star away (from observer / Earth)

hints: Hint 1: Think about what the word shift means for light - compare the wavelength you actually observe with the wavelength the star really emitted.
Hint 2: Recall what motion of a distant light source stretches light waves to longer wavelengths, similar to the Doppler effect for sound.
parts.proper_answer: Redshift is the increase in observed wavelength compared with the emitted (laboratory) wavelength, caused by the star moving away from the observer on Earth.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Is Shifted**
Light leaves the star with a particular wavelength fixed by atomic physics. By the time we receive it, that wavelength can appear changed. Redshift means: $$ \lambda_{observed} > \lambda_{emitted} $$ The whole pattern is moved toward the longer wavelength, red end of the spectrum.

Step 2: **Why It Happens**
This stretching happens because the source is receding from us. As the star moves away, successive wave crests have further to travel, so we receive them more spread out in space. That is the cosmological or Doppler redshift signature of a star moving away from Earth.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: Explain how cosmologists are able to determine that light from a distant star has undergone redshift.

markscheme_points.text: by examining the (lines in the) spectrum (of light from star)

hints: Hint 1: Remember that starlight is not a smooth continuum only - it contains sharp dark or bright lines due to specific atoms in the stellar atmosphere.
Hint 2: Think about what reference you would need in the laboratory to tell whether those lines have moved from their normal positions.
parts.proper_answer: Examine the absorption (or emission) lines in the spectrum of light from the star and compare their wavelengths with the known laboratory wavelengths for the same elements; a systematic shift to longer wavelength shows redshift.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use Spectral Lines as Fingerprints**
Each element produces lines at very precise wavelengths. When you disperse starlight with a spectrometer you see that same pattern of lines, but the whole pattern may be displaced.

Step 2: **Compare with Known Standards**
In the lab you measure the rest wavelengths for e.g. hydrogen or calcium. Then you line up the stellar spectrum alongside: $$ \text{redshift if } \lambda_{star} > \lambda_{lab} \text{ for the same line} $$ If every line is shifted by the same fractional amount to longer wavelength, you have confirmed redshift and can even calculate $z = \Delta\lambda / \lambda$.
